facts.statement: Bathornis was a flightless predator that occupied niches typically dominated by mammals.
facts.quote: Like the closely related and also extinct phorusrhacids, it was a flightless predator, occupying predatory niches in environments classically considered to be dominated by mammals.

facts.statement: Bathornis was a long-legged, short-winged bird with a large skull, resembling phorusrhacids in shape.
facts.quote: Overall, Bathornis is a long-legged, short-winged, large-skulled bird, similar in shape to phorusrhacids.

facts.statement: Bathornis species varied in size from those comparable to modern seriemas to animals reaching 2 meters in length.
facts.quote: Its numerous species span a large diversity of body sizes, ranging from forms about as large as modern seriemas to 2 m animals.

facts.statement: Bathornis was named "tall bird" because it was significantly larger than its modern seriema relatives.
facts.quote: The bird was noted as being massive in comparison to its modern seriema relatives, presumably the reason as to receive its genus name, "tall bird".

facts.statement: The species name "veredus" is a Latin word relating to speed, though its specific etymological explanation was not provided.
facts.quote: The species name, "veredus", is not given an explanation, though it is a Latin word relating to speed.

facts.statement: Bathornis is the most species-rich genus among all Cariamiformes, whether extinct or extant.
facts.quote: Bathornis is noted for its high number of species, and is the most speciose of all Cariamiformes, extinct or extant.

facts.statement: Bathornis was a carnivorous bird.
facts.quote: Bathornis was a carnivorous bird.

facts.statement: Bathornis grallator and B. veredus had strong beaks similar to phorusrhacids, with identical jugal reinforcement indicating similar biting stresses.
facts.quote: Bathornis grallator and Bathornis veredus showcase that it had a strong beak akin to that of phorusrhacids, even sharing an identical reinforcement of the jugal, implicating a similar biting stresses.

facts.statement: Large Bathornis species were likely apex predators that competed successfully with mammals for over 17 million years.
facts.quote: As Bathornis species reached large sizes, it is likely that they were apex predators within their environment, much as their South American phorusrhacid cousins; alongside the closely related Paracrax, they are examples of large predatory birds managing to compete successfully with mammals, having co-existed with large carnivorous mammals for over 17 million years.

facts.statement: A recent study suggests Bathornis is the sole representative of Bathornithidae, placing it outside the clade containing seriemas and phorusrhacids.
facts.quote: A recent phylogenetic study found Bathornis to be the sole representative of Bathornithidae, within Cariamiformes but outside of the clade composing seriemas and phorusrhacids.

facts.statement: A 2024 study finds Bathornis closer to seriemas than to phorusrhacids.
facts.quote: A 2024 study however finds Bathornis as closer to seriemas than phorusrhacids were.

facts.statement: Researchers caution that some sympatric Bathornis species might represent different sexes or morphs rather than distinct species.
facts.quote: Some caution has been suggested, given the possibility that some sympatric species might actually represent different sexes or morphs, though the vast temporal spanning of the genus still offers a large diversity.

facts.statement: Bathornis has a highly reduced first toe and a robust jugal, features possibly evolved convergently with phorusrhacids.
facts.quote: The bathornithid second toe is currently unknown, but the first toe is highly reduced, as with most Cariamiformes, and like phorusrhacids it possesses a robust jugal and reduced processus acrocoracoideus of coracoid, two features possibly having evolved in convergence due to their similar lifestyle.

facts.statement: Storrs Olson reassigned fossils originally interpreted as a terrestrial vulture to Bathornis in 1985.
facts.quote: Originally interpreted as a terrestrial cathartid, Storrs Olson reassigned it to Bathornis in 1985

facts.statement: Bathornis lived in various environments because of its long existence and many species.
facts.quote: Due to its longevity and high number of species, Bathornis spanned across several different types of environment.

facts.statement: The known range of Bathornis was located around the area that is now the Great Plains.
facts.quote: As a rule of thumb, however, its known range occurred around what is now the Great Plains

facts.statement: Recent analyses suggest that Bathornis likely preferred wetland environments.
facts.quote: However, more recent analyses conclude that it probably favoured wetland biomes.

facts.statement: The presence of Bathornis species near large mammals like Megacerops and Merycoidodon might indicate they preyed on them.
facts.quote: B. cursor is found in close association with Megacerops, and B. geographicus with Merycoidodon, which might imply predation on these mammals.

facts.statement: Bathornis shared its habitat with carnivorous mammals such as hyaenodontids, entelodonts, and nimravids, and competed with the bird Paracrax.
facts.quote: It shared its environment with several carnivorous mammals like hyaenodontids, entelodonts and nimravids, as well as the fellow cariamiform Paracrax, with which it would have competed.

facts.statement: There may be evidence that Bathornis and Paracrax avoided direct competition by living in different environments, with Paracrax in drier areas.
facts.quote: In particular, there may be evidence of niche partitioning with the latter, as it occurs in drier environments.

facts.statement: The genus Bathornis was named by Wetmore in 1927.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Bathornis (genus), Wetmore 1927

facts.statement: Bathornis belongs to the family Bathornithidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Bathornithidae

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Bathornis is Bathornis veredus.
facts.quote: Type species: Bathornis veredus

facts.statement: Bathornis lived from the Lutetian to the Burdigalian stages, between 45.9 and 18.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Lutetian to Burdigalian (45.9 to 18.5 million years ago)
